suggestions.title: Rear Window
suggestions.description: The highest-rated film on your list that has never been shown - 8.5, and one of only four Hitchcock films that appear on every serious all-time list. Your list has met Hitchcock once, with Psycho, which is horror: a knife, a shower, a scream. This is the other Hitchcock, the one who made suspense out of architecture and patience. L.B. 'Jeff' Jefferies is a news photographer in a Greenwich Village walk-up with a broken leg, a wheelchair, a telephoto lens and nothing to do but watch the courtyard. In summer heat, with the windows open, he watches his neighbours - Miss Lonelyhearts, the songwriter, Miss Torso, the newlyweds - and then he watches Lars Thorwald, travelling salesman, and becomes convinced the man's wife is no longer in the apartment. Grace Kelly's Lisa Fremont walks in as a woman trying to talk him out of his life and ends up on a fire escape in a stranger's apartment, and the film never lets you forget that every thrill you are enjoying is the thrill of being a peeping tom. Hitchcock built the entire courtyard on Stage 18 at Paramount: 31 apartments, twelve fully furnished with working water and electricity, with four permanent lighting rigs and remote switches in Jeff's apartment so he could cross-fade the whole world from dawn to night on command - the largest indoor set ever built at the studio at the time. The sound is famously reduced: no non-diegetic music inside the apartments, just a piano, a radio, a voice, and Franz Waxman's score arriving only where a score could exist in the world. One scene - Thorwald looking directly back into Jeff's lens - is the moment Hitchcock hands the audience its own guilt. If you have ever rated a thriller highly, this is the source most of them are drinking from.

suggestions.title: Grave of the Fireflies
suggestions.description: Your list is one of the strongest war collections on the internet - Schindler's List, Saving Private Ryan, Das Boot, Downfall, Apocalypse Now, Life Is Beautiful, The Pianist, Paths of Glory - and every single one of them looks at the war from the side of the adults fighting it, or the adults surviving it. This is the only canonical war masterpiece told from the point of view of two children on the losing civilian side, and it is animated, which has been your single biggest gap: Spirited Away and the Pixar films are the only animation ever shown here, and nothing from Studio Ghibli beyond Miyazaki. Isao Takahata - Miyazaki's partner and the studio's most uncompromising director - adapted Akiyuki Nosaka's semi-autobiographical 1967 story about a fourteen-year-old boy and his four-year-old sister after the firebombing of Kobe, and he opened the film with the ending: a boy dying in a train station, cards on the floor, 'September 21, 1945 - that was the night I died.' What follows is a flashback with no villain: the enemy is a collapsing system, an aunt's resentment, pride, rationing, and one tin of fruit drops. In Japan it was released in April 1988 as a double feature with My Neighbor Totoro - the most tonally sadistic pairing in film history - and the two films are a matching set: one about how children survive, one about how they don't. Takahata strips everything out; there is no fantasy, no expressive flourish, no rescue, and the fireflies of the title are the firebombs at the start and the memory of them at the end. Roger Ebert listed it as one of the great war films ever made and would not watch it again. Eighty-nine minutes, and it will stay far longer than anything else on your list. Be warned: this is the hardest film on this list and it does not soften.

suggestions.title: Dune: Part Two
suggestions.description: The payoff to the setup you were handed last round. Dune: Part One was the world-building - the first hour was deliberately political and slow so that the desert would mean something when the war arrived - and this is the war, and it is the reason that first film exists. Denis Villeneuve is now on your list four times, and this is where all of him is at once: the dread of Prisoners, the melancholy of Blade Runner 2049, the temporal patience of Arrival, all applied to Frank Herbert's novel about a young man who becomes a messiah and knows exactly what that will cost. Paul Atreides takes the Fremen's water and their war, and the film's central trick is that it is a revenge epic with a dread underneath: every cheer it earns is a cheer for the catastrophe coming in Part Three. The performances are the strongest in the trilogy - Timothee Chalamet finding the exact point where the boy stops being one, Javier Bardem's Stilgar turning faith into comedy and then horror, Austin Butler's Feyd-Rautha as a bald, black-toothed void, and Zendaya finally given a real part as Chani, the film's conscience. Greig Fraser shot the Harkonnen arena sequence in infrared black-and-white on a volcanic plain, and the sandworm-riding set piece was done on practical sand rigs so the scale is physical rather than rendered; Hans Zimmer threw out the orchestra for this one and leaned on drums, bagpipes and processed voices. It took two Oscars, for Sound and Visual Effects, from five nominations at the 97th Academy Awards, and it is the best large-scale studio film of the decade so far. Watch them back to back.
